findings.text: The first paragraph says what Athena is, who it is for and why it matters, in plain words. A newcomer can say what the project is without reading further.
findings.source: "Athena is an open-source system, written in Rust, that turns a short request into a change to a code repository... It solves the problem of AI edits that arrive unreviewed and unaccountable."

findings.text: The page lives at Athena's own address, but the title and heading are about a different project, firstmate. A newcomer who looks only at the heading may think the site is about firstmate. Only the lede below it makes clear that the page is a demonstration.

The top of the page links straight to next steps. That section lists the prerequisites, the clone and setup commands, and a first command (`athena ask "add a changelog"`), so the reader knows what to do next.
findings.source: "Next step: install Athena or read firstmate itself" and the Next steps section

findings.text: The lede promises two different models, but the prerequisites name only Claude Code. They do not say where the second model comes from, or whether an API key or paid account is needed. That leaves the cost of trying Athena unclear.
findings.source: "has one AI model do the work and a different one check it" vs. Next steps: "either Claude Code or npm (to install Claude Code)"

findings.text: The page never shows Athena's main product: a traced commit with its cost and verdict. The whole page shows the separate 'study' feature instead, so a newcomer has to take the core claim on trust.
findings.source: "get back a commit they can trace to the request, the models, the cost and the verdict"

findings.text: This link appears near the top for every visitor, but a newcomer is not the owner. It is unclear what it is or whether they should click it.
findings.source: "Owner view: proposals waiting for your decision"

findings.text: Most of the page is a dense state-machine study of firstmate, with terms like 'yolo', 'captain', 'exit 75' and 'pending-close record'. It is well defined and fully cited, but heavy for a newcomer who came to learn about Athena. The 'Start here' section helps by giving a short version first.
findings.source: Sections "States of a piece of work", "Transitions" (t1–t12), "Claims and sources" (45 claims)

findings.text: The page is honest about what it did not check: nothing was run, and every claim comes from reading the source. This makes the 'traced to lines' promise more believable.
findings.source: Limits of this study, f1: "no failure or retry edge was observed; every claim is marked read"

findings.text: This closing note refers to an internal repository folder that a newcomer cannot see from the page, so it tells them nothing useful.
findings.source: About this page: "the name of the folder under studies/ that holds the data this page is generated from"
